strengths: Clear problem identification: Demonstrates that coherency degradation in steering is undetectable by standard metrics (MMLU, PPL) and proposes a well-motivated solution

Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple analytical levels (layer-wise, head-wise, ablation studies), comprehensive metrics (trait, coherency, MMLU, PPL, IFEval), and strong human evaluation validation (92.8% agreement)
Technically sound geometric analysis approach using cosine similarity heatmaps and head contribution scores to efficiently identify persona-related components without prohibitive causal interventions

Consistent and clear empirical improvements: Head Cor steering achieves best Pareto frontiers in 11/12 conditions for Qwen2.5-7B and demonstrates superior trait-coherency trade-offs across all six personas

Excellent presentation with comprehensive visualizations, detailed appendices including qualitative examples, and novel Right-normalized Constrained Envelope Area metric for multi-objective evaluation
Practical significance for safer LLM deployment: Demonstrates functional modularity in transformers with implications for safer alignment and component-level control
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding: Paper identifies that 3 heads specialize in persona control but provides no mechanistic explanation for why or how this specialization emerges; the noise amplification hypothesis is intuitive but untested

Significant generalization concerns: Only two dense models tested (both GQA); Appendix F reveals Gemma3 shows fundamentally different behavior (multiple direction shifts vs. single transition); MoE results underdeveloped; different behavior for safety-related personas suggests post-training effects follow different mechanisms

Incomplete related work comparisons: No empirical evaluation against Angular Steering or Dynamic Steering despite mentioning these methods; only compares intervention points, not against alternative approaches to addressing coherency degradation

Architectural dependency limitations: Method requires per-model/per-architecture head identification; unclear if findings generalize beyond the tested models; Grouped Query Attention may be crucial for observed specialization

Mixed performance for safety-related traits: Section 5.3 shows Attn Residual outperforms Head Cor on MMLU/IFEval for safety personas, indicating harmful behaviors involve broader circuits beyond identified heads; limits utility for critical safety applications

Methodological concerns: Head identification threshold not formally defined; steering coefficient ranges differ between conditions (0.5-10.0 vs 0.5-14.0), confounding comparisons; human evaluation limited to 60 samples without significance testing; dot product metric (Eq. 4) loses directional information

Limited mechanistic insight: Lacks investigation of what these heads actually compute (attention patterns, feature properties); missing connections to sparsity and lottery ticket literature; no analysis of head attention patterns or learned representations

strengths: Addresses real practical problem: coherency degradation in activation steering is genuine and underexplored
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: dual model validation, human-LLM agreement (92%+), systematic Pareto frontier analysis across six personas
Systematic identification methodology: layer-wise cosine similarity combined with head-wise contribution scores provides clear pipeline
Ablation studies confirm functional specialization: zero ablation shows identified heads are causally important for persona control
Consistent empirical results: Head Cor achieves favorable trait-coherency trade-offs across tested conditions (Table 1)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core finding that targeted intervention produces less noise than broad intervention is unsurprising; identifies which heads but not why they emerged

Poor generalization: only 2 dense models tested; authors acknowledge Gemma3 shows fundamentally different layer-wise behavior (multiple sharp transitions vs. single transition), falsifying generality claims

Unvalidated core hypothesis: claims about 'off-target noise amplification' lack direct evidence; alternative explanations (OOD steering effects, vector properties) unexplored; no comparison to noise-reduction baselines

Methodological concerns: circular head identification (layer-wise then head-wise steering); Head Contribution Score assumes linearity in nonlinear attention; Head Cor+Anti underperformance suggests incomplete geometric understanding

Generalization gaps: tied to difference-in-means extraction method (unknown transfer to CAA/SAEs); only 6 personas tested (hallucination behaves differently); only dense architectures (MoE only briefly mentioned); no large models (13B+) tested

Evaluation issues: LLM-as-Judge may be biased and coherency is subjective; custom metric (Right-normalized Constrained Envelope Area) appears designed to favor proposed method; temperature inconsistency (1.0 vs 0.0) across metrics
Modest practical improvements: Table 1 shows gains are often small (e.g., 18.2→25.8); some configurations show competitive performance from other methods; practical significance unclear

Shallow mechanistic insight: paper identifies what happens but not why; why exactly 3 heads across both models?; no explanation for why identified heads maintain style without hurting coherency; speculative 'abstract high-level heads' discussion

Incomplete analysis: role consistency of heads across personas not thoroughly examined; ablation only sequential in one direction; no individual head importance ranking; sensitivity to hyperparameters not explored
Ethical concerns: paper amplifies harmful personas (evil, hallucinating, sycophant) with limited discussion of misuse potential or safety implications

strengths: Addresses critical practical problem: coherency degradation in activation steering, showing disconnect from standard metrics (MMLU, PPL, IFEval)
Systematic discovery methodology combining layer-wise cosine similarity and head-wise contribution scores efficiently identifies Style Modulation Heads without expensive causal interventions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 personas across 2 model architectures, asymmetric degradation phenomenon documented, human evaluation validates LLM-as-Judge (~92.8% agreement)
Rigorous empirical design with Pareto frontier analysis, sequential ablation studies confirming functional specialization, validation that interventions don't degrade knowledge/instruction-following
Strong empirical results: Head Cor steering outperforms baselines in 11/12 cases (Qwen) and 9/12 cases (Llama), particularly effective for trait suppression (Target−α)
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-designed figures, comprehensive appendices with detailed methodology, persona prompts, and evaluation protocols
High reproducibility: detailed experimental setup, hyperparameters in tables, system prompts provided, code promised
Interesting mechanistic insight about sparse head specialization with implications for architecture design and parameter efficiency
weaknesses: Limited architectural generalization: only 2 dense models thoroughly tested; critical finding that Gemma3 shows multiple sharp direction shifts (unlike Qwen/Llama) suggests architectural sensitivity; claims of generality somewhat overstated

Limited persona diversity: only 6 personas with some artificially constructed; hallucination uses different layer due to safety fine-tuning, suggesting alignment-heavy traits follow different mechanisms not fully explored

Safety-related divergence (Section 5.3): Head Cor underperforms on MMLU/IFEval for harmful persona amplification, indicating entanglement with factual reasoning that contradicts claimed orthogonality to knowledge

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: identifies WHAT but not WHY; minimal analysis of attention patterns or what heads compute; connection to known head functions unexplored; Head Cor+Anti underperformance unexplained
Scope limited to difference-in-means steering: findings untested with CAA, linear probing, SAEs, or other extraction methods; unclear transferability to alternative steering approaches

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars despite 5-run averaging; Pareto comparisons lack uncertainty quantification; reliance on LLM-as-Judge (GPT-4.1-mini) leaves room for bias

Missing comparisons: no direct comparison with Angular Steering or Dynamic Steering variants mentioned as related work; would strengthen claims to benchmark against recent coherency mitigation methods

Practical limitations underexplored: still requires 200 samples for vector extraction; method for identifying heads for novel personas unclear; computational cost of localization not discussed; head identification not tested on unseen personas

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical obstacle (coherency degradation in activation steering)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 personas, 2 primary models + 2 extended models, multiple metrics with human validation (91-92% agreement)
Elegant geometric analysis approach for localizing steering targets without exhaustive search
Strong and consistent empirical results with clear Pareto frontier improvements (Head Cor wins 11/12 conditions on Qwen2.5-7B)
Rigorous experimental design with appropriate ablations (causal verification, random controls, cross-run averaging)
Excellent reproducibility with 42-page appendices including prompts, protocols, and implementation details
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging architectural sensitivity and scope constraints
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core insight (precise intervention reduces noise) is intuitive; execution is straightforward application of existing geometric analysis techniques

Serious generalizability concerns acknowledged in Section 7: Style Modulation Heads localization breaks down for larger models (Gemma-3-12B, Qwen3-30B) with multiple layers containing relevant heads and different architectural patterns; undermines broad claims about generality
Narrow application scope restricted to persona/style control; unclear if findings generalize to other steering targets (factual knowledge, reasoning, safety behaviors), limiting impact

Shallow mechanistic understanding: paper identifies 'where' to steer but not 'why' these heads are specialized or what information they process; no connection to known attention head functions (induction, copying)

Incomplete baseline comparisons: mainly compares intervention locations (residual stream variants) rather than alternative coherency-improvement methods (Angular Steering, Dynamic Steering, SAE-based approaches mentioned but not benchmarked)
Experimental bias: Head Cor tested with larger coefficient range (α ∈ [0.5, 14.0]) vs. others (α ∈ [0.5, 10.0]) with post-hoc justification; enables comparison bias

Missing failure mode analysis: underdeveloped discussion of when Head Cor underperforms (e.g., safety personas on Llama-3.1-8B for MMLU/IFEval); no characterization of persona properties enabling this approach
No statistical significance testing: 5 runs reported but no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or p-values; LLM-judge validation on small sample (10 pairs × 3 judges)
Persona vector quality dependency on contrastive prompts not analyzed for robustness; GPT-5 used to generate some prompts with minimal documentation

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a genuine practical problem in activation steering with compelling empirical evidence of coherency collapse
Rigorous experimental methodology with comprehensive evaluation across 6 personas, 2 base models, and human validation achieving 92.8% agreement on trait expression
Systematic layer-wise and head-wise analysis with proper ablation studies demonstrating functional specialization of identified heads
Strong empirical results showing consistent Pareto frontier improvements for head-level steering across evaluation conditions
Exceptional reproducibility with extensive appendices, detailed prompts, evaluation protocols, and promised code release
weaknesses: Critical generalizability failure: The core finding (3 specific heads solving coherency) breaks down for architecturally diverse models. Gemma-3-12B shows multiple sharp transitions unlike Qwen/Llama; Qwen3-MoE shows no clear localization. No principled method exists to identify heads in novel architectures, severely limiting practical applicability

Insufficient theoretical understanding: The paper cannot explain why identical heads work across 6 unrelated personas, what computational function these heads perform, or mechanistically validate the central 'off-target noise amplification' hypothesis. The approach is empirically validated but theoretically opaque

Evaluation limitations: Coherency is measured via subjective LLM-as-judge scoring without direct comparison to alternative coherency-preserving methods (Angular Steering, Dynamic Steering, In-Distribution Steering). No evaluation of whether improvement comes from head localization or simply being more conservative with steering coefficients

Limited scope: Only tested with difference-in-means steering and linear Activation Addition. No evaluation with alternative vector extraction methods (CAA, SAEs). Unclear if findings generalize beyond this narrow steering paradigm

Methodological concerns: The head contribution score (Eq. 4) is task-specific yet yields identical heads across diverse personas—suggesting either metric bias or unexplained deep phenomenon. Layer identification uses architecture-dependent heuristics (cosine similarity threshold) that fail for other architectures. Arbitrary threshold choices (τ=80.0) lack sensitivity analysis

strengths: Identifies and characterizes a genuine, under-appreciated problem: coherency degradation in activation steering that standard metrics fail to capture
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, plus extended testing on Gemma-3 and Qwen3-MoE) with six diverse personas
Robust evaluation methodology combining LLM-as-judge with human validation (92.8% agreement), addressing the key limitation that standard benchmarks miss coherency collapse
Sound technical approach using layer-wise cosine similarity analysis and head contribution scores to systematically identify persona-responsible components
Practical solution with clear implementation path: targeting specific heads demonstrably reduces coherency degradation while maintaining trait control (Pareto frontier analysis in Section 5.2)
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (Section 7), including architectural sensitivity that could undermine generalizability claims
Well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (heatmaps, Pareto frontiers) and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic insight: the paper shows that specific heads matter but does not explain why these particular heads (and why exactly 3?) handle persona, or how intervening on them reduces noise amplification in practice

Significant generalization limitations documented in Appendix F: Gemma-3-12b-it shows trait-dependent multiple transition points rather than single localization; Qwen3-MoE lacks clear transition layers; these findings suggest reduced applicability to larger/different-architecture models despite 'robust' framing in title

Somewhat incremental contribution building directly on Chen et al. (2025)'s persona vector approach; the main novelty (head-specific steering) is useful but represents incremental methodological progress rather than fundamental advancement
Heavy reliance on a specific steering approach (difference-in-means); unclear whether findings generalize to other vector extraction or steering methods, limiting broader applicability
Head contribution metric (Eq. 4) uses dot product favoring larger-norm heads, though validation via cosine similarity shows consistent results; theoretical justification for this choice is lacking
Missing deeper mechanistic analysis: no investigation of what these heads attend to, how they interact, or why the pattern holds across different personas and models
Evaluation scope limitations: only 10 human-evaluated pairs per persona (modest sample), restricted to instruction-tuned models, and only 6 personas tested; scope of generalization unclear
